claim: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) supports dendritic translation in neurons.
source: While the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) supports dendritic translation, most dendrites lack the Golgi apparatus (GA), an essential organelle for conventional secretory trafficking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about neuronal cell biology.

claim: Most dendrites lack the Golgi apparatus (GA).
source: While the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) supports dendritic translation, most dendrites lack the Golgi apparatus (GA), an essential organelle for conventional secretory trafficking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The Golgi apparatus is an essential organelle for conventional secretory trafficking.
source: While the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) supports dendritic translation, most dendrites lack the Golgi apparatus (GA), an essential organelle for conventional secretory trafficking.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cellular secretory pathways.

claim: Following ER exit, GluA1 undergoes spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway.
source: Following ER exit, the AMPA-type glutamate receptor GluA1 and neuroligin 1 undergo spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway and accumulate in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Following ER exit, neuroligin 1 undergoes spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway.
source: Following ER exit, the AMPA-type glutamate receptor GluA1 and neuroligin 1 undergo spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway and accumulate in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: GluA1 accumulates in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
source: Following ER exit, the AMPA-type glutamate receptor GluA1 and neuroligin 1 undergo spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway and accumulate in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing colocalization and co-trafficking.

claim: Neuroligin 1 accumulates in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
source: Following ER exit, the AMPA-type glutamate receptor GluA1 and neuroligin 1 undergo spatially restricted entry into the dendritic secretory pathway and accumulate in recycling endosomes (REs) located in dendrites and spines before reaching the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: GluA1 surface delivery occurred even when GA function was disrupted.
source: Surprisingly, GluA1 surface delivery occurred even when GA function was disrupted.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by BFA experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Recycling endosomes mediate forward secretory trafficking in neuronal dendrites and spines through a specialized GA-independent trafficking network.
source: Thus, in addition to their canonical role in protein recycling, REs also mediate forward secretory trafficking in neuronal dendrites and spines through a specialized GA-independent trafficking network.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experimental approaches including BFA treatment and dominant-negative Rab11.

claim: mRNAs encoding thousands of different proteins are found in dendrites.
source: Indeed, mRNAs encoding thousands of different proteins are found in dendrites (Cajigas et al., 2012), where their regulated translation is critical for neuronal dendrite development, maintenance and plasticity (Sutton and Schuman, 2006; Bramham and Wells, 2007; Hanus and Schuman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cajigas et al., 2012.

claim: Regulated translation of dendritic mRNAs is critical for neuronal dendrite development, maintenance and plasticity.
source: Indeed, mRNAs encoding thousands of different proteins are found in dendrites (Cajigas et al., 2012), where their regulated translation is critical for neuronal dendrite development, maintenance and plasticity (Sutton and Schuman, 2006; Bramham and Wells, 2007; Hanus and Schuman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sutton and Schuman, 2006; Bramham and Wells, 2007; Hanus and Schuman, 2013.

claim: Many dendritic mRNAs encode secreted factors and critical integral membrane proteins.
source: Intriguingly, many of these dendritic mRNAs encode secreted factors and critical integral membrane proteins, implying the presence of a satellite secretory system for local processing and trafficking of newly synthesized cargo.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivates the study, based on known mRNA localization patterns.

claim: Nascent proteins synthesized in the soma can enter dendritic compartments through lateral diffusion in the ER membrane.
source: In addition to locally translated proteins, nascent proteins synthesized in the soma can also enter dendritic compartments through lateral diffusion in the ER membrane (Cui-Wang et al., 2012), or by active transport (Valenzuela et al., 2014), since the ER network is contiguous throughout the somatodendritic domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cui-Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Nascent proteins synthesized in the soma can enter dendritic compartments by active transport.
source: In addition to locally translated proteins, nascent proteins synthesized in the soma can also enter dendritic compartments through lateral diffusion in the ER membrane (Cui-Wang et al., 2012), or by active transport (Valenzuela et al., 2014), since the ER network is contiguous throughout the somatodendritic domain.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Valenzuela et al., 2014.

claim: The ER network is contiguous throughout the somatodendritic domain.
source: In addition to locally translated proteins, nascent proteins synthesized in the soma can also enter dendritic compartments through lateral diffusion in the ER membrane (Cui-Wang et al., 2012), or by active transport (Valenzuela et al., 2014), since the ER network is contiguous throughout the somatodendritic domain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by the cited references.

claim: Most dendrites (~80%) lack Golgi apparatus (GA).
source: In contrast, most dendrites (~80%) lack Golgi apparatus (GA), a defining organelle of the cellular secretory network that mediates canonical post-ER trafficking (Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Torre and Steward, 1996; Gardiol et al., 1999; Hanus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Torre and Steward, 1996; Gardiol et al., 1999; Hanus et al., 2016.

claim: Cargo exiting the dendritic ER is initially directed to ER-Golgi intermediate compartments (ERGICs).
source: Previous studies demonstrate that cargo exiting the dendritic ER is initially directed to ER-Golgi intermediate compartments (ERGICs), a collection of tubulovesicular membranes distributed throughout all dendrites (Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Hanus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Hanus et al., 2014.

claim: ERGICs are a collection of tubulovesicular membranes distributed throughout all dendrites.
source: Previous studies demonstrate that cargo exiting the dendritic ER is initially directed to ER-Golgi intermediate compartments (ERGICs), a collection of tubulovesicular membranes distributed throughout all dendrites (Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Hanus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krijnse-Locker et al., 1995; Hanus et al., 2014.

claim: The ERGIC network normally shuttles proteins between the ER and GA.
source: The ERGIC network normally shuttles proteins between the ER and GA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ERGIC function.

claim: ERGIC membranes mediate bi-directional trafficking at the ER-Golgi boundary.
source: In addition to mediating bi-directional trafficking at the ER-Golgi boundary (Ben-Tekaya et al., 2005), ERGIC membranes are also reported to physically interact with recycling endosomes (REs) (Marie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ben-Tekaya et al., 2005.

claim: ERGIC membranes physically interact with recycling endosomes (REs).
source: In addition to mediating bi-directional trafficking at the ER-Golgi boundary (Ben-Tekaya et al., 2005), ERGIC membranes are also reported to physically interact with recycling endosomes (REs) (Marie et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marie et al., 2009.

claim: A number of secretory proteins traffic through REs on their initial voyage to the PM.
source: A number of secretory proteins traffic through REs on their initial voyage to the PM, and some cargoes, such as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance receptor (CFTR), may enter the RE network in a GA-independent manner (Yoo et al., 2002; Marie et al., 2009; Grieve and Rabouille, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoo et al., 2002; Marie et al., 2009; Grieve and Rabouille, 2011.

claim: CFTR may enter the RE network in a GA-independent manner.
source: A number of secretory proteins traffic through REs on their initial voyage to the PM, and some cargoes, such as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance receptor (CFTR), may enter the RE network in a GA-independent manner (Yoo et al., 2002; Marie et al., 2009; Grieve and Rabouille, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoo et al., 2002; Marie et al., 2009; Grieve and Rabouille, 2011.

claim: REs are broadly distributed throughout dendrites, including within a large fraction of dendritic spines.
source: The broad dendritic distribution of REs, including within a large fraction of dendritic spines, makes them well suited to mediate forward trafficking to the plasma membrane with high spatial precision, perhaps at the level of individual synapses (Cooney et al., 2002; Park et al., 2004; Kennedy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cooney et al., 2002; Park et al., 2004; Kennedy et al., 2010.

claim: 3xFM-GluA1 strongly colocalizes with an engineered ER marker (TfR-KDEL) prior to addition of DDS.
source: Prior to addition of DDS, 4xFM-NL1 strongly colocalizes with an engineered ER marker (TfR-KDEL) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Following addition of 1 µM DDS, 4xFM-NL1 rapidly redistributes to the perinuclear GA and ultimately to the cell surface.
source: Following addition of 1 µM DDS, 4xFM-NL1 rapidly redistributes to the perinuclear GA and ultimately to the cell surface (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Without DDS, the distribution of 3xFM-GluA1 closely resembled the endogenous ER-marker BIP.
source: Without DDS, the distribution of 3xFM-GluA1 closely resembled the endogenous ER-marker BIP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Adding DDS triggered robust accumulation of 3xFM-GluA1 in the GA.
source: Adding DDS triggered robust accumulation of 3xFM-GluA1 in the GA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Very low background levels of 3xFM-GluA1 were observed on the cell surface prior to release.
source: We observed very low background levels of 3xFM-GluA1 on the cell surface prior to release and robust surface delivery following ER-release (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Robust surface delivery of 3xFM-GluA1 occurred following ER-release.
source: We observed very low background levels of 3xFM-GluA1 on the cell surface prior to release and robust surface delivery following ER-release (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: 4xFM-SEP-NL1 was efficiently delivered to the cell surface of neurons following addition of DDS.
source: 4xFM-SEP-NL1 was also efficiently delivered to the cell surface of neurons following addition of DDS (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Significant surface delivery of GluA1 was detectable within two hours following ER-release.
source: Significant surface delivery was detectable within two hours following ER-release for both cargoes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-course data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Maximum surface delivery levels of NL1 were reached at four hours following ER-release.
source: Maximum levels were reached at four and eight hours for NL1 and GluA1 respectively (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-course data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Maximum surface delivery levels of GluA1 were reached at eight hours following ER-release.
source: Maximum levels were reached at four and eight hours for NL1 and GluA1 respectively (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-course data in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Following delivery to the PM, both GluA1 and NL1 localized to dendrites and spines.
source: Following delivery to the PM, both GluA1 and NL1 localized to dendrites and spines, consistent with previous reports using similarly tagged expression constructs and their associated fluorescent proteins were sensitive to thrombin treatment (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 3) (Chih et al., 2006; Patterson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures, and supported by citations.

claim: Locally photoconverted 3xFM-mEOS-GluA1 displayed limited mobility in the absence of DDS.
source: Locally photoconverted 3xFM-mEOS-GluA1 (hereafter referred to as mEOS*-GluA1) displayed limited mobility in the absence of DDS, consistent with effective clustering and ER retention by the FM domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: When DDS was added, mEOS-GluA1* exited the ER and accumulated in nearby trafficking organelles.
source: In contrast, when we added DDS, mEOS-GluA1* exited the ER and accumulated in nearby trafficking organelles (Video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Video 1.

claim: Two hours after dendritic photoconversion and ER-release, 12.9 ± 3.0% of the photoconverted signal returned to the neuronal soma.
source: Two hours after dendritic photoconversion and ER-release, we observed that most mEOS*-GluA1 redistributed to trafficking organelles within dendrites, with only 12.9 ± 3.0% (mean ± SEM, n = 9 neurons from 3 experiments) of the photoconverted signal returning to the neuronal soma (Figure 2A,C).
evidence: This is quantified data from experiments shown in Figure 2A,C.

claim: When mEOS-GluA1 was locally photoconverted in the soma, 93.3 ± 3.3% of mEOS*-GluA1 redistributed to the somatic GA following ER release.
source: Similarly, when we locally photoconverted mEOS-GluA1 in the soma, the vast majority (93.3 ± 3.3%; mean ± SEM; n = 7 neurons from 3 experiments) of mEOS*-GluA1 redistributed to the somatic GA following ER release with negligible signal reaching even proximal dendritic regions (Figure 2B–C; Video 2).
evidence: This is quantified data from experiments shown in Figure 2B-C and Video 2.

claim: AMPA receptors enter distinct downstream trafficking organelles depending on the cellular domain from which they exit the ER.
source: Thus, AMPA receptors enter distinct downstream trafficking organelles depending on the cellular domain from which they exit the ER.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photoconversion experiments showing spatial segregation.

claim: Cargo leaving the dendritic ER accumulated in dendritic puncta with kinetics that closely matched the accumulation of GluA1 signal in the somatic GA in the same cells.
source: Interestingly, cargo leaving the dendritic ER accumulated in dendritic puncta with kinetics that closely matched the accumulation of GluA1 signal in the somatic GA in the same cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mEOS*-GluA1 preferentially accumulated at organelles close to or within the initial photoconverted region with a length constant of 11.6 µm.
source: This analysis revealed that mEOS*-GluA1 preferentially accumulated at organelles close to or within the initial photoconverted region with a length constant (i.e. distance over which the photoconverted signal decreases to 63.2% relative to the edge of the photoconverted region) of 11.6 µm (Figure 3B,C; n = 5 neurons from 3 experiments).
evidence: This is quantified data from experiments shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: After somatic photoconversion, minimal entry of mEOS*-GluA1 into dendritic puncta was observed.
source: Conversely, after somatic photoconversion, we observed minimal entry of mEOS*-GluA1 into dendritic puncta (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Robust accumulation of newly released GluA1 in the somatic GA occurred under 20°C temperature block conditions.
source: Indeed, we observed robust accumulation of newly released GluA1 in the somatic GA under these conditions (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cargo stalled in punctate dendritic organelles in nearly every dendritic branch at 20°C.
source: However, we also observed cargo stalling in punctate dendritic organelles in nearly every dendritic branch (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dendritic GluA1 puncta that arose following ER release did not colocalize with classical cis- (GM130) or trans-GA markers (TGN38).
source: Accordingly, the dendritic GluA1 puncta that arose following ER release did not colocalize with classical cis- (GM130) or trans-GA markers (TGN38) even though the somatic GA was strongly labeled for both markers (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERGIC membranes are distributed throughout the dendritic arbor.
source: In agreement with this study, we observed ERGIC membranes throughout the dendritic arbor (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: The 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 puncta that formed early following ER release strongly colocalized with ERGIC53.
source: We also observed that the 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 puncta that formed early following ER release strongly colocalized with ERGIC53, detected either by antibody staining for endogenous p58 (rat homologue of ERGIC53) or by expressing GFP-ERGIC53 (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Colocalization between GFP-ERGIC53 and 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 peaked ~50–60 min following ER-release.
source: Colocalization between GFP-ERGIC53 and 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 peaked ~50–60 min following ER-release, and declined as cargo progressed through the secretory network (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course colocalization data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Transport from the somatic GA to the dendritic arbor (especially proximal regions) can occur.
source: Thus, transport from the somatic GA to the dendritic arbor (especially proximal regions) can also occur. (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the photobleaching recovery experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Frequent juxtaposition of ERGIC and TfR puncta was observed throughout the dendritic arbor.
source: Using standard confocal microscopy, we observed frequent juxtaposition of ERGIC and TfR puncta throughout the dendritic arbor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: The spatial proximity of ERGIC and TfR puncta was not simply due to chance.
source: Despite their high density, this was not simply due to chance as a randomized, but equally dense, set of RE coordinates did not exhibit the same spatial proximity to ERGIC (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by randomization analysis shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: ERGIC structures range in diameter from ~60 nm to ~400 nm in dendrites.
source: We observed ERGIC structures, ranging in diameter from ~60 nm (the resolution limit in the far-red channel, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) to ~400 nm in diameter, widely distributed throughout dendrites (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by STED imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: ERGIC membranes were often observed immediately adjacent to TfR-positive structures.
source: ERGIC membranes were often observed immediately adjacent to TfR-positive structures (Figure 5F), consistent with the possibility of functional coupling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by STED imaging data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Robust colocalization of TfR and GluA1 was observed 120 min following addition of DDS.
source: We observed robust colocalization of TfR and GluA1 120 min following addition of DDS (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Before ER-release, mobile REs were almost never positive for 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 (1/77 for Rab11-labeled REs, 0/60 for TfR-labeled REs).
source: Before ER-release, numerous mobile REs could be observed, but these were almost never (1/77 for Rab11-labeled REs, 0/60 for TfR-labeled REs) positive for 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is quantified data from photobleaching assays shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: One hour following ER-release, 32.2 ± 5.5% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with TfR-GFP.
source: In contrast, one hour following ER-release, 32.2 ± 5.5% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with TfR-GFP and 37.1 ± 5.5% co-traffic with GFP-Rab11.
evidence: This is quantified data from photobleaching assays shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: One hour following ER-release, 37.1 ± 5.5% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with GFP-Rab11.
source: In contrast, one hour following ER-release, 32.2 ± 5.5% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with TfR-GFP and 37.1 ± 5.5% co-traffic with GFP-Rab11.
evidence: This is quantified data from photobleaching assays shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: After 150 min following ER-release, 52.9 ± 6.7% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with TfR-GFP.
source: After 150 min, these numbers increased to 52.9 ± 6.7% for TfR-GFP and 59.9 ± 4.3% for GFP-Rab11 (Figure 6D,E, Video 4; mean ± SEM, n = 6–8 neurons/timepoint/marker from 3 experiments).
evidence: This is quantified data from photobleaching assays shown in Figure 6D,E and Video 4.

claim: After 150 min following ER-release, 59.9 ± 4.3% of GluA1-containing vesicles co-traffic with GFP-Rab11.
source: After 150 min, these numbers increased to 52.9 ± 6.7% for TfR-GFP and 59.9 ± 4.3% for GFP-Rab11 (Figure 6D,E, Video 4; mean ± SEM, n = 6–8 neurons/timepoint/marker from 3 experiments).
evidence: This is quantified data from photobleaching assays shown in Figure 6D,E and Video 4.

claim: Thrombin had no effect on the extent of Rab11/GluA1 co-trafficking following ER release.
source: However, thrombin had no effect on the extent of Rab11/GluA1 co-trafficking following ER release supporting a prominent role for REs in forward trafficking in dendrites (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantified data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 48.9 ± 3% of Rab11 vesicles contained 4xFM-mCh 2.5 hr post-release.
source: We observed nearly identical co-trafficking of 4xFM-mCh and GFP-Rab11 as we did with 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 and GFP-Rab11 (48.9 ± 3% of Rab11 vesicles contained 4xFM-mCh 2.5 hr post-release; mean ± SEM; n = 8 neurons from 2 experiments), indicating that RE-mediated forward trafficking in dendrites applies to soluble as well as integral membrane secretory cargoes (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is quantified data from experiments shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: RE-mediated forward trafficking in dendrites applies to soluble as well as integral membrane secretory cargoes.
source: We observed nearly identical co-trafficking of 4xFM-mCh and GFP-Rab11 as we did with 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 and GFP-Rab11 (48.9 ± 3% of Rab11 vesicles contained 4xFM-mCh 2.5 hr post-release; mean ± SEM; n = 8 neurons from 2 experiments), indicating that RE-mediated forward trafficking in dendrites applies to soluble as well as integral membrane secretory cargoes (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both soluble (4xFM-mCh) and membrane (GluA1) cargoes co-traffic with Rab11.

claim: NL1 entered the RE network soon after ER-release.
source: We further confirmed the generality of this trafficking route using a different synaptic protein NL1, which also entered the RE network soon after ER-release (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-trafficking data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: 67 ± 8% of SEP-GluA1 fusion events occurred in the dendritic arbor vs. 33 ± 8% in the soma.
source: We observed that 67 ± 8% of fusion events occurred in the dendritic arbor vs. 33 ± 8% in the soma (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is quantified data from SEP-GluA1 insertion event imaging shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: REs are present in 48% of dendritic spines.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed REs throughout dendrites, including within 48% of dendritic spines, the major postsynaptic compartments of excitatory synapses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Cooney et al., 2002; Kennedy et al., 2010).
evidence: This is quantified data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: ERGIC membranes only rarely localize to spines.
source: In contrast, ERGIC membranes only rarely localize to spines (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 was detectable within 20.6 ± 3.7% of RE-positive spines 150 min following ER release in the presence of thrombin.
source: We found that 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 was detectable within 20.6 ± 3.7% of RE-positive spines vs only 4.8 ± 2.1% in control (no ER release) conditions (Figure 6K; mean ± SEM, n = 5 neurons/condition from 2 experiments, p=0.006 unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test.).
evidence: This is quantified data from experiments shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Spines harboring REs accumulated more surface GluA1 than neighboring spines lacking REs.
source: Accordingly, when we surface labeled mCh-GluA1 receptors 120 min following ER release, we observed that spines harboring REs accumulated more surface GluA1 than neighboring spines lacking REs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3) consistent with a role for REs in local delivery of secretory cargo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Nearly every (97 ± 3%) dendritic spine that contained GFP-SP also contained an RE marked by TfR-mCh.
source: Intriguingly, nearly every (97 ± 3%; mean ± SEM, 554 RE-containing spines from 4 neurons) dendritic spine that contained GFP-SP also contained an RE marked by TfR-mCh (although not all RE-containing spines contained GFP-SP).
evidence: This is quantified data from imaging experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Rab11(S25N) significantly impaired surface delivery of 3xFM-GluA1 compared to Rab11(WT) or mCh alone at 2 and 4 hr after DDS addition.
source: Rab11(S25N) significantly impaired surface delivery of 3xFM-GluA1 compared to Rab11(WT) or mCh alone at the earliest time points we can detect appreciable surface GluA1 accumulation (2 and 4 hr after DDS addition) (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Rab8(T22N) did not significantly affect GluA1 surface delivery at 2 hr following ER release.
source: We observed that Rab8(T22N) did not significantly affect GluA1 surface delivery at an early timepoint (2 hr) following ER release, but significantly impaired surface delivery at a later (4 hr) timepoint (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Rab8(T22N) significantly impaired GluA1 surface delivery at 4 hr following ER release.
source: We observed that Rab8(T22N) did not significantly affect GluA1 surface delivery at an early timepoint (2 hr) following ER release, but significantly impaired surface delivery at a later (4 hr) timepoint (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Dominant negative Rab5 (S34N) had no effect on GluA1 surface delivery.
source: Finally, we tested dominant negative Rab5 (S34N mutation), which is critical for early endosome function, and observed no effect on surface delivery (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: BFA caused a rapid (<20 min) and complete dispersal of the somatic Golgi.
source: To verify the efficacy of our BFA treatment, we imaged live neurons expressing galactosyl transferase fused to mEmerald (GalT-mEm). BFA caused a rapid (<20 min) and complete dispersal of the somatic Golgi (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: ERGIC membranes and REs remained intact following BFA treatment.
source: In contrast, ERGIC membranes and REs remained intact following BFA treatment (Figure 8B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: Robust co-trafficking of 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 and TfR-GFP was observed following BFA treatment.
source: In contrast, when we conducted the same experiment in cortical neurons, we observed robust co-trafficking of 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 and the RE marker TfR-GFP, followed by the delivery of a significant fraction of GluA1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by photobleaching assay data shown in Figure 8G,H.

claim: A significant fraction of GluA1 was delivered to the plasma membrane following BFA treatment.
source: In contrast, when we conducted the same experiment in cortical neurons, we observed robust co-trafficking of 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 and the RE marker TfR-GFP, followed by the delivery of a significant fraction of GluA1 to the plasma membrane (Figure 8G,H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: BFA had no effect on the percentage of dendritic 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 co-labeled with TfR 60 min following the temperature shift to 37°C.
source: Intriguingly, BFA had no effect on the percentage of dendritic 3xFM-mCh-GluA1 co-labeled with TfR 60 min following the temperature shift to 37 ˚C (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantified data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: A significant reduction in the fraction of TfR vesicles positive for GluA1 was observed in BFA-treated cells.
source: Not surprisingly, we did observe a significant reduction in the fraction of TfR vesicles positive for GluA1, indicating that some fraction of RE-localized cargo is derived from BFA-sensitive GA (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantified data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The level of GluA1 surface delivery was reduced to 25.3 ± 3.8% of control cells in BFA-treated cells, but still 2.4-fold over background levels.
source: Accordingly, the level of GluA1 surface delivery was reduced in BFA-treated cells (25.3 ± 3.8% of control cells without BFA), but still 2.4-fold over background levels (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is quantified data from surface labeling experiments shown in Figure 8H.

claim: A substantial fraction of GluA1 enters the RE network and is trafficked to the cell surface in a GA-independent manner in neurons.
source: Together, these data indicate that in neurons, a substantial fraction of GluA1 enters the RE network and is trafficked to the cell surface in a GA-independent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BFA experiments showing continued trafficking despite GA disruption.

claim: Both NL1 and VSV-G surface expression was fully blocked by BFA.
source: In contrast to GluA1, we observed that both NL1 and VSV-G surface expression was fully blocked by BFA indicating that not all cargoes follow the same trafficking route in neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface labeling data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 4.

claim: Colocalization of mEOS*-GluA1 and TfR-HT(JF646) was observed in the same dendritic branches that were initially photoconverted.
source: Live imaging over the next 150 min revealed colocalization of mEOS*-GluA1 and TfR-HT(JF646) in the same dendritic branches that were initially photoconverted (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Little accumulation of mEOS*-GluA1 was observed in the somatic GA over the time course of the photoconversion experiment.
source: Importantly, we observed little accumulation of mEOS*-GluA1 in the somatic GA over the time course of the experiment.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the photoconversion experiments shown in Figure 8I.

claim: Dendritic secretory cargo is spatially constrained as it progresses from ER to ERGIC to REs.
source: Thus, dendritic secretory cargo is spatially constrained as it progresses from ER to ERGIC to REs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photoconversion experiments showing local trafficking.

claim: The majority (88 ± 1%) of surface GluA1 was sensitive to endoH.
source: Consistent with previous work, we observed that the majority (88 ± 1%; mean ± SEM 4 independent experiments) of surface GluA1 and a significant fraction of GluA2 (40 ± 3%, mean ± SEM 5 independent experiments) were sensitive to endoH, further supporting a GA-bypass route for endogenous proteins (Figure 9C) (Hanus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is quantified data from endoH sensitivity experiments shown in Figure 9C and supported by citation.

claim: A significant fraction (40 ± 3%) of surface GluA2 was sensitive to endoH.
source: Consistent with previous work, we observed that the majority (88 ± 1%; mean ± SEM 4 independent experiments) of surface GluA1 and a significant fraction of GluA2 (40 ± 3%, mean ± SEM 5 independent experiments) were sensitive to endoH, further supporting a GA-bypass route for endogenous proteins (Figure 9C) (Hanus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is quantified data from endoH sensitivity experiments shown in Figure 9C and supported by citation.

claim: TARPγ8 in the same biochemical preparation was completely endoH resistant.
source: In contrast to AMPA receptors, TARPγ8 in the same biochemical preparation was completely endoH resistant, consistent with our data demonstrating that not all synaptic cargoes follow a GA-independent trafficking route to the cell surface (Figure 9C and Figure 8—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by endoH sensitivity data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Synaptic proteins exiting the dendritic ER undergo spatially restricted trafficking to dendritic ERGICs.
source: Our findings reveal that synaptic proteins exiting the dendritic ER undergo spatially restricted trafficking to dendritic ERGICs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the photoconversion and colocalization experiments.

claim: Following ERGIC accumulation, cargo next appears in dendritic REs, which are critical for subsequent PM delivery.
source: Following ERGIC accumulation, cargo next appears in dendritic REs, which are critical for subsequent PM delivery.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the co-trafficking and dominant-negative Rab11 experiments.

claim: Dendritic secretory cargo trafficking to REs and the PM could occur even when the GA was disrupted.
source: Intriguingly, we observed that dendritic secretory cargo trafficking to REs and the PM could occur even when the GA was disrupted.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the BFA experiments.

claim: Dendritic secretory cargo can undergo direct, local trafficking through a unique secretory network involving ERGICs and REs, but bypassing the GA.
source: Thus, dendritic secretory cargo can undergo direct, local trafficking through a unique secretory network involving ERGICs and REs, but bypassing the GA (Figure 10).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence and illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: Synthesis of integral membrane proteins and secreted factors can occur locally in dendrites.
source: While synthesis of integral membrane proteins and secreted factors can occur locally in dendrites, it was unclear whether dendritic secretory organelles could spatially coordinate local delivery of these proteins to nearby dendritic sites.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Nascent proteins are able to diffuse within the ER.
source: This issue is further complicated by the fact that nascent proteins are able to diffuse within the ER (Cui-Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cui-Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Dendritic ER can undergo morphological plasticity to spatially restrict lateral diffusion.
source: While dendritic ER can undergo morphological plasticity to spatially restrict lateral diffusion, it was unknown whether proteins are similarly spatially constrained after they exit the ER and traffic through subsequent secretory organelles.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: A significant fraction of VSV-G is shuttled towards the somatic GA following ER exit.
source: Previous studies using the vesicular stomatitis viral glycoprotein (VSV-G) to investigate the dendritic secretory network report that following ER exit, a significant fraction of dendritic pre-Golgi vesicle carriers are shuttled towards the somatic GA, suggesting that spatial information may be lost as cargo exits the ER (Horton and Ehlers, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Horton and Ehlers, 2003.

claim: A fraction of VSV-G is locally trapped in ERGIC structures following ER exit.
source: However, more recent studies report local trapping of a fraction of VSV-G in ERGIC structures following ER exit, supporting the possibility of a local secretory network (Chen et al., 2013; Hanus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013; Hanus et al., 2014.

claim: The synaptic proteins GluA1 and NL1 follow the same initial itinerary as VSV-G.
source: Importantly, we find that the synaptic proteins GluA1 and NL1 follow the same initial itinerary as VSV-G, revealing a general dendritic trafficking principal that applies to diverse secretory cargoes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all three cargoes accumulate in dendritic ERGICs.

claim: The trafficking itineraries of NL1 and VSV-G diverge from GluA1 following ERGIC accumulation.
source: However, based on the BFA sensitivity of NL1 and VSV-G surface expression, their trafficking itineraries must diverge from GluA1 following ERGIC accumulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential BFA sensitivity observed for these cargoes.

claim: The dendritic and somatic trafficking networks are strikingly segregated.
source: We also made the surprising observation that the dendritic and somatic trafficking networks were strikingly segregated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the photoconversion experiments showing minimal crosstalk.

claim: The downstream organelles and processing of secretory proteins largely depends on their location of ER exit.
source: Thus, the downstream organelles and processing of secretory proteins largely depends on their location of ER exit, which would have a major impact on post-translational modifications such as N-linked glycosylation (Hanus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial segregation observed in the photoconversion experiments and supported by citation.

claim: Dendritic cargo trafficked to mobile vesicles positive for the RE markers TfR and Rab11 following ERGIC accumulation.
source: Following ERGIC accumulation, we observed that dendritic cargo trafficked to mobile vesicles positive for the RE markers TfR and Rab11.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the co-trafficking experiments.

claim: The RE network plays a central role in recycling proteins to and from the PM.
source: While the RE network plays a central role in recycling proteins to and from the PM, it has also been reported to mediate anterograde secretory trafficking of a number of different proteins in other cell types (Ang et al., 2004; Lock and Stow, 2005; Cancino et al., 2007; Thuenauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: REs have been reported to mediate anterograde secretory trafficking of a number of different proteins in other cell types.
source: While the RE network plays a central role in recycling proteins to and from the PM, it has also been reported to mediate anterograde secretory trafficking of a number of different proteins in other cell types (Ang et al., 2004; Lock and Stow, 2005; Cancino et al., 2007; Thuenauer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ang et al., 2004; Lock and Stow, 2005; Cancino et al., 2007; Thuenauer et al., 2014.

claim: REs play a critical role in integrating synaptic activity to regulate the protein composition of the neuronal plasma membrane.
source: In neurons, REs are widely distributed throughout dendrites, where they play a critical role in integrating synaptic activity to regulate the protein composition of the neuronal plasma membrane (Park et al., 2004; Lasiecka and Winckler, 2011; Kennedy and Ehlers, 2011; Esteves da Silva et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Park et al., 2004; Lasiecka and Winckler, 2011; Kennedy and Ehlers, 2011; Esteves da Silva et al., 2015.

claim: Synaptic proteins, such as AMPA receptors can undergo basal and activity-induced recycling through the RE network.
source: While synaptic proteins, such as AMPA receptors can undergo basal and activity-induced recycling through the RE network, our findings expand the role of dendritic REs to include anterograde trafficking of newly secreted synaptic cargo molecules.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about AMPA receptor trafficking.

claim: The dendritic RE network is spatially restricted near clusters of dendritic spines.
source: Because REs are mobile, it is unclear whether the spatial distribution of cargo leaving the ER and ERGIC network is preserved once it accesses REs, but previous studies suggest that the dendritic RE network is spatially restricted near clusters of dendritic spines (Cooney et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cooney et al., 2002.

claim: REs migrate into dendritic spines in an activity-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, REs migrate into dendritic spines in an activity-dependent manner where they may regulate synaptic properties (Esteves da Silva et al., 2015; Park et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Esteves da Silva et al., 2015; Park et al., 2006.

claim: REs could maintain and regulate dendritic and synaptic properties through constitutive delivery of newly synthesized integral membrane and secreted proteins.
source: Our data indicate that REs could maintain and regulate dendritic and synaptic properties through constitutive delivery of newly synthesized integral membrane and secreted proteins, including to a select subset of synapses via spine-resident REs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of GluA1 accumulation in spine REs and differential surface delivery.

claim: A subset of cargo molecules, including CFTR, connexins and the drosophila anti-PS1 integrin can traffic to the cell surface without traversing the GA.
source: Previous reports indicate that a subset of cargo molecules, including CFTR (Yoo et al., 2002), connexins (Martin et al., 2001) and the drosophila anti-PS1 integrin (Schotman et al., 2008) can traffic to the cell surface without traversing the GA.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yoo et al., 2002; Martin et al., 2001; Schotman et al., 2008.

claim: GluA1 released from dendritic ER could access the local RE network even in BFA-treated cells where the somatic GA was disrupted.
source: To assess whether dendritic ER cargo can bypass the GA, we performed our trafficking assays in the presence of BFA to disrupt GA function. We found that GluA1 released from dendritic ER could still access the local RE network, even in BFA-treated cells where the somatic GA was disrupted.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the BFA experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Trafficking of secretory cargo from dendritic ERGIC to REs and to the PM is completely blocked at 20°C.
source: Similar to classic GA temperature block experiments, trafficking of secretory cargo from dendritic ERGIC to REs and to the PM is completely blocked at 20 ˚C, (Matlin and Simons, 1983), indicating that dendritic ERGICs and the somatic GA share some properties.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the temperature block experiments and supported by citation to Matlin and Simons, 1983.

claim: The somatic GA was rapidly and robustly dismantled following BFA treatment.
source: However, the somatic GA was rapidly and robustly dismantled following BFA treatment, while dendritic ERGICs remained intact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 8A-D.

claim: Dendritic ERGICs remained intact following BFA treatment.
source: However, the somatic GA was rapidly and robustly dismantled following BFA treatment, while dendritic ERGICs remained intact.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data shown in Figure 8B-D.

claim: A diverse cohort of synaptic receptors, channels and cell adhesion proteins present on the neuronal cell surface lack mature N-glycosylation.
source: Whether dendritic ERGICs harbor the same secretory processing enzymes as somatic GA remains an intriguing and open question, but our data support a previous study demonstrating that a diverse cohort of synaptic receptors, channels and cell adhesion proteins present on the neuronal cell surface lack mature N-glycosylation, a hallmark of GA processing (Hanus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hanus et al., 2016 and by the endoH sensitivity data in Figure 9.

claim: Local secretory processing in dendrites may yield an exclusive repertoire of posttranslational modifications that could uniquely impact protein structure and function.
source: Thus, local secretory processing in dendrites may yield an exclusive repertoire of posttranslational modifications that could uniquely impact protein structure and function.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the observation of GA-independent trafficking and immature glycosylation.
